rv.q: Looks like it was worth every penny.
And it turns out that a boxing musical wasn’t such a crazy notion, after all.
For a show that on many levels is a miss, that climactic sequence is a thrilling knockout.

And it becomes apparent that the musical Rocky subscribes to the method of Mamma Mia! – the previous piece of cheese to take over this theatre, the Winter Garden, for aeons – for ensuring a hit: wallop the audience for the final 15 minutes.

Although the performances by Karl and Margo Seibert, as his wallflower of girlfriend, Adrian, offer authentic moments of tenderness, they are let down by Stephen Flaherty and Lynn Ahrens’s surprisingly tin-eared score, and the frequently movie-parroting book by Thomas Meehan and Sylvester Stallone.
But there is a sweet center here: Karl, who imbues the Cinderella-guy story with enormous reserves of macho sensitivity and the big heart that denizens of the South Philly gym keep describing.
Rocky the Musical is a solid if unremarkable adaptation that delivers the expected emotional punches without much surprise.
At this point, "Rocky" is trying to be immersive. The cost is its soul.

Unfortunately, this two-character, black-and-white kitchen-sink drama, reminiscent of Paddy Chayefsky in his made-for-TV days, is trapped inside (and eventually strangled by) a garishly colorful bloated mess of an unmusical musical called Rocky.
This musical version of the beloved underdog boxing movie feels more like a bout between a bantamweight and a heavyweight
In other words, "Rocky" is indeed a knockout.
Rocky delivers edge-of-your-seat thrills that underscore the fact that fans of boxing and live theater share some DNA.
Rocky is a show that punches above its weight class, delivering an emotionally satisfying evening
He carries the show effortlessly, boxes like a champ, and sings just as heroically.
For whatever its flaws, “Rocky” the musical wins with a knockout final scene that is, guaranteed, unlike anything you’ve seen in the theater.

The sequence, choreographed by Steven Hoggett, relies on a spectacular scenic surprise that changes the way you look at the production. But to "go the distance," to quote the fictional Balboa, a musical needs more than a stunning climax.
Karl gets a vigorous workout and emerges triumphant.
But other numbers mix predictable sentiments with overheated rock accents.
It's a triumph that, theatrically speaking, is pretty hollow.
At last, after two lackluster hours, “Rocky” finally delivers suspense, excitement, drama!
In effect, “Rocky” is the new “Spider-Man,” a similarly flashy and misconceived spectacle-musical that exists mainly to showcase an elaborate fight sequence as its finale.

cn.t: Critics praise Rocky's spectacular final boxing sequence and technical wizardry, but find the first act slow with a forgettable score. Andy Karl's performance impresses, though the show relies heavily on its thrilling 15-minute climax.
